newsitem.title: FINLAND: PENSION FUNDS' BOURSE INVESTMENT MAY DOUBLE - PURO.
newsitem.headline: PENSION FUNDS' BOURSE INVESTMENT MAY DOUBLE - PURO.

text.p: Finnish pension funds' investments in the stockmarket may double following changes in the private pension funding system proposed by a committee on Wednesday, the committee chairman Kari Puro said.
He told a news conference that private pension funds now have about seven percent of pension liabilities -- 126.0 billion markka at end-1995 -- invested in the stockmarket.
This proportion could double if funds' working capital were increased to eight percent of liabilities to work as a buffer for stockmarket volatility, as the committee proposes, he said.
But this would still not be a significant increase, he said.
In 1995, pension funds' working capital totalled 6.8 billion markka or 5.4 percent of pension liabilities.
"We have a rough estimate that ... such a change in working capital could in 5-10 years double the amount of bourse investment," Puro said.
The Helsinki bourse's end-October market capitalisation was 250.3 billion markka.

The Puro committee's proposal was welcomed on Wednesday by Minister of Social and Healthcare Sinikka Monkare who said she was convinced the government agreed with her that the proposal's main recommendations should be carried out.
She vowed to start immediate work to ensure that key legislation would be in force at the turn of the year.

Unions and employers also welcomed the proposal, but the small and medium size company lobby -- the Finnish Entrepreneurs -- said it would increase pressure on small firms to set up a pension fund of their own since it gave no clue of how the sector's access to pension money would be granted.
The proposal included two main points -- a total reform of the system and a near-term change to make possible an increase in working capital without lifting pension contributions.
Puro said the reform would remove the link between the minimum return requirement and current contributions.
This would allow working capital to fluctuate with asset values without changing pensions or contributions.

Based on this change, the committe proposed that pension insurers' minimum required rate of return would be lowered to five percent in 1997 from six percent currently, and that the rate of funding be temporarily lowered to three percent, and then return to par with the return requirement.

The temporary two percentage point difference between the funding rate and the required return would be in force two or three years, and this is how working capital would be increased, the proposal said.
